Why Nutrition Labels Matter

The Nutrition Facts panel on packaged foods is one of the most powerful tools available for making informed food choices. Yet many people find it confusing, overwhelming, or simply ignore it altogether. Understanding how to read a nutrition label does not require a degree in nutrition science. It requires knowing where to look and what matters most for your individual health goals.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requires most packaged foods to carry a Nutrition Facts label. The updated format, which became mandatory in 2020, makes several key pieces of information easier to find and understand.

Start with Serving Size

The first thing to check is the serving size at the top of the label. All the nutritional information listed below it corresponds to this specific portion. Many packages contain multiple servings, which means eating the entire package means consuming two, three, or even more times the listed amounts.

For example, if a bag of chips lists a serving size of 15 chips with 150 calories, but you eat 30 chips, you have actually consumed 300 calories. The updated labels now include both per-serving and per-package information for products that could reasonably be consumed in one sitting.

Calories in Context

Calories tell you how much energy a serving provides. The general guideline of 2,000 calories per day is used as a reference on labels, but individual needs vary based on age, sex, activity level, and health goals. Rather than fixating on calorie counts, use them as a general guide to compare similar products.

Nutrients to Limit

The label highlights several nutrients that most Americans should consume less of: added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat. Added sugars are now listed separately from total sugars, making it easier to see how much sugar has been added during processing versus what occurs naturally in ingredients like fruit or milk.

The American Heart Association recommends limiting added sugars to no more than 25 grams per day for women and 36 grams for men. For sodium, the recommended limit is 2,300 milligrams per day. Checking these values can help you make more informed choices between similar products.

Nutrients to Get Enough Of

The updated label also highlights nutrients that many Americans do not get enough of: dietary fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, and potassium. Choosing products higher in these nutrients supports bone health, digestive health, blood pressure regulation, and overall well-being.

The Ingredient List

Ingredients are listed in descending order by weight. The first few ingredients make up the bulk of the product. If sugar, corn syrup, or another sweetener appears in the first three ingredients, the product is likely high in added sugars. Look for whole, recognizable ingredients near the top of the list.

Marketing Claims to Question

Terms like "natural," "wholesome," and "made with real fruit" are marketing terms with little regulatory definition. Even "organic" does not necessarily mean a product is low in sugar, sodium, or calories. Always check the actual Nutrition Facts panel rather than relying on front-of-package marketing claims.

Key Takeaways

  • Always check the serving size first, as all numbers are based on it
  • Compare added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat between similar products
  • Look for fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, and potassium
  • Read the ingredient list for whole, recognizable ingredients
  • Do not rely on front-of-package marketing claims alone
description: A practical guide to understanding the Nutrition Facts panel, ingredient lists, and common marketing claims on food packaging.
title: Reading Nutrition Labels: What to Actually Look For
